what_this_is: The five CSOAI verifiability checks applied to ten frontier model providers' OWN published evaluation artifacts - system cards, model cards, safety and preparedness reports. Our published third-party census covers fifteen evaluators and no model provider. System cards are the only evaluation artifacts a regulator can now compel: EU AI Act Article 53 obligations for general-purpose AI models have been fine-backed since 2 August 2026. Each check is answerable by fetching public bytes with no cooperation from the subject. No lab was contacted.
what_this_is_not: Not a ranking. There is no score, no league table and no ordering. Five columns, states in cells.
Not a certification. We measure; we never certify.

Not a judgement of safety, of research quality, or of whether a lab's evaluations are good ones. A lab can do excellent safety work and answer NO on every column here. These checks ask whether a reader can verify what was published, not whether what was published is true.
Not an Article 53 compliance assessment. Nothing here says whether any lab meets a legal obligation.
Not complete. Ten providers, on one day, on the artifacts each one's own index led to.

checks.signed: Is any published evaluation result cryptographically signed, with a resolvable public key?
checks.content_addressed: Is a published result identified by a digest of its own bytes, cited by the publisher?
checks.bank_published: Are the questions or tasks behind a published score available to read?
checks.corrections: Is there a public record of errors the lab found in its OWN published results - and when a named third-party evaluator later corrects a number the card cites, does the card change?
checks.recomputable: Can a third party reproduce a published score from published artifacts without contacting them?

state_meanings.PARTIAL: true in a stated scope and not in another; both halves recorded
state_meanings.NO: checked and absent; the places searched are recorded
state_meanings.UNCHECKABLE: could not be determined from public sources. NOT the same as NO.

rulings_applied: A version string, a date, an arXiv version number or a human-readable filename is NOT a content address.

A digest the publisher never cites is at most PARTIAL. The reader supplying the pin does not count as the publisher committing to one. This ruling is already applied to METR, Arena, LiveBench and HELM in the third-party census and is applied unchanged here - which is why Anthropic's SHA-1 CDN paths and Hugging Face's LFS sha256 oids are PARTIAL and not YES.
Reusing a third party's public bank (MMLU, GPQA, SWE-bench) is not the lab publishing its bank; it is PARTIAL at most, and the distinction is recorded in the cell.
A git log or a commit history is a change record, not a declared erratum. It supports PARTIAL, not YES.
Signature absence is claimed only after a binary scan of the bytes for /Sig, /ByteRange and adbe.pkcs7, never from the absence of a signature page.
method_limitations: The Internet Archive was INTERMITTENTLY OFFLINE throughout the measurement window. web.archive.org/cdx returned an 'Internet Archive: Temporarily Offline' HTML page at 12:31Z, 12:33Z, 12:40Z and 12:48Z, and HTTP 429 at 12:36Z, but served valid JSON between roughly 12:35Z and 12:40Z. The xAI and Mistral sweep obtained real CDX JSON in that window and its findings rest on data actually received; the OpenAI/Microsoft and Google DeepMind/Meta sweeps did not, and for them the Wayback silent-revision test could not be run at all. Where a sweep could not run it, the question is recorded as UNCHECKABLE rather than NO. No Wayback error page was ever treated as a result.

Substitutes were used where Wayback was unavailable: HTTP last-modified against the document's own printed date, in-band PDF /CreationDate and /ModDate, in-document changelog sections, git and Hugging Face commit histories, and arXiv version histories. These can establish THAT bytes changed at a stable URL; without an archived copy they cannot establish WHAT changed. The Google DeepMind corrections cell rests on this weaker form of evidence and says so.

The last-modified substitute is INVALID on deploymentsafety.openai.com, where the origin returns last-modified equal to CDN cache-fill time: three different cards reported last-modified within one second of the request, and gpt-6-astra reported a value equal to request time minus its own age header. That line of evidence was discarded rather than reported.

openai.com/index/* returns HTTP 403 to curl even with a browser User-Agent. System cards were read from deploymentsafety.openai.com, which does answer. System cards published only in blog form on openai.com/index/ were not examined.

Only 11 of the 26 model slugs on deploymentsafety.openai.com serve a PDF at /<slug>/<slug>.pdf; the rest return HTML there. For those, rendered HTML was scanned and NO claim is made about the signature state of any PDF form of those cards. Its sitemap.xml is also emitted with http://localhost:4321/ hostnames, a build defect; paths were used with the real host substituted, so any page whose real path differs would have been missed.

x.ai HTML pages are Cloudflare-blocked to both curl and WebFetch (x.ai/sitemap.xml, x.ai/news, x.ai/model-card and data.x.ai/ all returned 403). Those paths are UNCHECKABLE, not absent; xAI artifacts were reached only as direct PDF URLs and the artifact set was enumerated via Wayback CDX rather than via xAI's own index.

trust.mistral.ai returns HTTP 200 but is JS-rendered and yielded only a page title; its contents are UNCHECKABLE, not absent. developer.meta.com's sitemap returns HTTP 403, so Meta's surface could not be enumerated from a sitemap.

qwen.ai, moonshot.ai and kimi.com are JS-rendered SPAs with catch-all routing that return HTTP 200 with app HTML for ANY path, so absence of a page cannot be inferred from a status code there, and their /.well-known/security.txt 200s are catch-alls rather than real files. Content rendered only client-side on those hosts is UNCHECKABLE.

Meta's Hugging Face repos are gated (gated:'manual'); the commits API and paths-info both return HTTP 401, so Meta's HF-side revision history and LFS sha256 oids could not be read from public bytes at all. The public GitHub mirror meta-llama/llama-models was used instead and may diverge from the HF card.

GitHub code and repository SEARCH was unavailable: gh api search/repositories returned HTTP 422 'User flagged as spammy' for the authenticated account. Whether Qwen's in-house banks (QwenSWEBench, CoWorkBench, RecreationBench, ClawEval-MM, NL2Repo-Bench) exist anywhere on GitHub is therefore UNCHECKABLE, not NO. The Hugging Face half of that search did run and returned none.

PDF text extraction is lossy on kerned table cells. This was confirmed empirically on the Kimi K2 tech report, where 36 of 37 benchmark rows appeared to change between arXiv v1 and v2 and every difference proved to be an extraction artifact. Every number-change claim in this census rests on a normalised comparison, never on a raw diff. Numbers rendered only inside images or vector-drawn charts - including MAI-Transcribe-1's WER figures and Mistral's Shieldstral safety charts - are invisible to this method.

Signature checking covered security.txt, the downloaded PDFs' internals, GitHub release assets and Hugging Face repo trees. It did NOT cover detached signatures published out of band: a keyserver, a Sigstore transparency log, or ModelScope, which DeepSeek and Qwen also mirror to. Every SIGNED: NO means absent from the surfaces checked.

Coverage is the current flagship line plus predecessors. DeepSeek has 105 Hugging Face models, Qwen 465 and Moonshot 19; those 589 repos were not all tree-scanned, and Mistral's file lists were enumerated for 4 of more than 100 repos. A signature in an unsampled repo would not have been seen.

No Microsoft Responsible AI Transparency Report PDF was downloaded or scanned; no claim is made about its signature or corrections state. Azure AI Foundry Transparency Notes on learn.microsoft.com were read from server-rendered HTML (100,765 chars, no benchmark percentages found); numbers rendered client-side could not be ruled out.

One lead was chased to a conclusion and cleared rather than reported: OpenAI's GPT-5 system card cites METR's 50% time horizon as 'around 2h15m (65m - 4h30m 95% CI)', while METR's live report at https://metr.org/evaluations/gpt-5-report/ (fetched 2026-09-17T12:49Z) headlines 'around 2 hours 17 minutes'. The card's figure appears verbatim in the evaluator's current text. Whether METR's March 2026 regularisation correction later moved this particular figure is UNCHECKABLE with Wayback down, but no divergence between card and evaluator is visible today.
No lab was contacted. Every cell is from public bytes fetched between 2026-09-17T12:31Z and 2026-09-17T12:50Z.
notable_findings: SIGNED is NO for all ten. Not one frontier lab cryptographically signs any published evaluation result. 100-plus PDFs were binary-scanned for /Sig, /ByteRange and adbe.pkcs7 across the ten subjects with zero hits. The only PGP-signed artifact found anywhere is OpenAI's /.well-known/security.txt, a vulnerability-disclosure contact record, whose key resolves only from the origin the file itself names. Microsoft publishes an OpenPGP key for CSAF security advisories and does not sign model cards. The industry that asks to be trusted on measurement signs its bug-report inbox and not one measurement.

The Anthropic accidental content address HOLDS, and is broader than reported. All 34 PDFs fetched from www-cdn.anthropic.com have a 40-hex path component exactly equal to the SHA-1 of their bytes - as the filename in 29 cases and as a directory in 5, including the current Claude Opus 5 system card at ceaf5c7ff2783855203fde8208ec311252dced5b. It is not limited to the Claude 4 and 4.1 cards. It is a real content address, in a hash function broken for collision resistance since 2017, that no reader is told to rely on; the string 'sha1' appears once on /system-cards, inside CMS metadata for an Open Graph image. Anthropic also serves identical bytes under a non-addressed path on assets.anthropic.com and links THAT one from the Transparency Hub.

Because of that accidental content address, three distinct byte-versions of the Claude 4 system card are simultaneously live and distinguishable, which is how the census's sharpest corrections finding became visible at all. One of them carries a Changelog: 'September 2, 2025 - Fixed incorrect evaluation numbers for Claude Code Impossible Tasks', and its footnote 29 states the correction ran 'from 5% to 19% for Claude Opus 4 and from 10% to 7% for Claude Sonnet 4'. As of 2026-09-17, https://www.anthropic.com/system-cards still links the UNCORRECTED version showing 5% and 10%, on the same index page that links the Claude Opus 4.1 addendum showing the corrected 19% and 7%.

Meta is the census's confirmed case of a named evaluator's correction failing to reach the card. https://ai.meta.com/blog/llama-4-multimodal-intelligence/ still reads 'an experimental chat version scoring ELO of 1417 on LMArena' and hyperlinks to https://lmarena.ai/leaderboard, which today lists llama-4-maverick-17b-128e-instruct at rank 107 with rating 1145.28 - 272 Elo points lower - with the experimental variant no longer present at all. Meta's page carries no editor's note seventeen months later.

xAI's case is different from a stale number and arguably worse: two published artifacts were silently regenerated about two days after publication, at unchanged date-stamped URLs still reading 'Last updated: August 20, 2025', and the edit DELETED the UK AI Security Institute's attribution and its adverse finding that 'an un-safeguarded version of Grok 4 poses a plausible risk of assisting a non-expert in the creation of a chemical or biological weapon'. The numeric tables were untouched. A census that only compares numbers would have seen nothing.
Only OpenAI answers YES on corrections, and the disclosure has a seam: the same correction is published as '0.4% to 1.5%' in the GPT-5.6 card and '0.4% to 1.48%' in the GPT-5.5 card.

Anthropic's /system-cards index, the page its own sitemap advertises, stops at Claude Opus 4.5 (November 2025). System cards for Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, Mythos Preview, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 are published and reachable through the Transparency Hub and through stable slugs, and none is listed on the index.

Google DeepMind overwrites model-card PDFs in place at stable URLs without updating the date printed on the card. Gemini-2-5-Pro-Model-Card.pdf reads 'Model card updated June 27, 2025' against bytes last written 2025-10-07; Gemini-2-0-Flash-Model-Card.pdf reads 'published April 15, 2025' against bytes written 2025-12-18. A reader citing either card cannot know which bytes they read. Its Frontier Safety Framework reports also attribute all external results to anonymous 'third party evaluator(s)', so the named-evaluator correction test cannot be run against DeepMind at all.

Moonshot's Kimi-K3 ships machine-readable eval records at .eval_results/*.yaml whose source.url points back at the model card that states the number - a provenance field that cites itself. They were added by Hugging Face staff pull requests merged by Moonshot. It is the clearest illustration in this census of why a content address has to come from the publisher.
